DISPATCH_COMMAND ($1403)
Purpose: Find the rule matching the current verb and noun and run its action script. Scans the two-byte verb-rule table for the verb, then requires the following byte to be the any-noun wildcard $FB or to equal the parsed noun; on a match it loads the script and runs the interpreter.
Inputs: VERB_ID ($4C), NOUN_ID ($4D); the verb-rule table base is the word at $199E; ACTION_SCRIPT_COUNT ($2A12) bounds the rule index.
Outputs: On a match, RUN_ACTION_SCRIPT sets SCRIPT_PC and RUN_SCRIPT executes the bytecode. On no match, sentence $03 is printed and the caller's return address is discarded so control unwinds directly to the outer parse loop. A rule index at or above the count returns silently.
Assumptions: The rule index doubles as the action-script index, so the table order and the script table order must agree. The bit-7 test on the index rejects indices above 127 before the count comparison.

Outputs: A = the byte; SCRIPT_PC incremented across the page boundary; flags reflect the load.

Purpose: Map a parsed noun token to the object it names. Subtracts the noun token base $32, scans the noun-to-object map for that value, and returns the object's current location together with its icon slot index.
Inputs: A = parsed noun token; NOUN_TO_OBJECT_INDEX ($22A4) is an $FF-terminated map from object slot to noun value.
Outputs: On success carry is set, A holds OBJECT_LOCATIONS[slot], Y holds the object slot index and CURRENT_OBJECT_INDEX ($5C) holds the icon slot index. On failure carry is clear and A is meaningless.
Assumptions: Carry is part of the API: callers must not treat A as a location when carry is clear. The map index and the location index are the same value, while the icon index is the map position, so the three id spaces are deliberately distinct.

RUN_SCRIPT ($1605)
Purpose: The bytecode interpreter. Reads opcodes at SCRIPT_PC: values $80 and above are conditions dispatched through the condition table, values below $80 are actions dispatched through the action table, $FE separates rules and $FF ends the script. A false condition skips forward to the next separator.
Inputs: SCRIPT_PC ($4E/$4F) points at a script; the condition table base is the word at $1191 and the action table base is the word at $0DE1.
Outputs: The script has been executed to its terminator, or control has left through one of the non-local exits ($0FC9, $0FDD, $0FF1). Any game state, display state or disk state may have changed.
Assumptions: Both dispatches work by writing the handler address into the operand bytes of a JSR instruction ($1642/$1643 for conditions, $169A/$169B for actions), so the interpreter is self-modifying and not reentrant. Interrupts do not enter it, and handlers that unwind must do so through the documented non-local exits. When an action opcode of $80 or above is encountered in the action position, the interpreter backs SCRIPT_PC up by one and re-reads it as a condition.
Clobbers: A, X, Y, flags, WORK_PTR ($0C/$0D), SCRIPT_PC, the four self-modified operand bytes, and everything the invoked handlers clobber.
Hardware changes: None directly; handlers reach the VIC-II, CIA, colour RAM, keyboard and disk.

script PRINT_ROOM_DESCRIPTION runs ($148C) on each pass of MAIN_LOOP ($0409).
This is interpreted data, not 6510 code. RUN_SCRIPT ($1605) walks it through SCRIPT_PC
($4E/$4F). Opcodes $80-$89 are conditions, dispatched through CONDITION_DISPATCH_TABLE
($1193); each returns carry, and a false condition jumps to the skip loop at $169F, so
consecutive conditions AND together. Opcodes $00-$7F are actions via ACTION_DISPATCH_TABLE
($0DE3). $FE separates rules, $FF ends the script.
What it does each turn:
- once only (OBJ_FLAGS[6]), sets Atreyu's strength OBJ_COUNTERS[1] = 50 and lights flag 7
- warns at strength 10 (sentence $1B) and kills at 0 (sentence $1C, pause, RESTART)
- grants OBJ_FLAGS[$11] while the Black Velvet Cape (object $1A) is carried
- keeps flag 7 set while the Glowglobe (object $13) is carried; flag 7 is the same "room
lit" flag DESCRIBE_CURRENT_ROOM ($107E) tests before printing anything
- counts turns in the dark in OBJ_COUNTERS[6] and kills at 4 (sentence $41)
- drains strength each turn while poisoned (OBJ_FLAGS[8], sentence $40)
It ends with action $07 (RETURN_SKIP_CALLER), which pops the interpreter's self-modified JSR
frame and returns straight to PRINT_ROOM_DESCRIPTION, so the trailing $FF is unreachable.
Being below $2F00, it survives every part load: the PART1/2/3 overlays cover $2F00-$96FF
only.

TOKEN_POINTERS_TABLE — 94 little-endian pointers, one per compressed-text dictionary token.
A prose byte with bit 7 set is a token reference: the renderer clears bit 7, doubles the
remaining 0..93 id and reads the word at TOKEN_POINTERS_TABLE + 2*id. The pointer addresses a
dictionary record, so ids $80-$DD are defined and $DE-$FF have no entry in this occupant.
The 94 pointers occupy $25DD-$2698; the records they address begin immediately afterwards at
$2699 (WORD_THE_LC) and run to $28B8.

Compressed-text dictionary records, $2699-$28B8. Each record is one length byte followed by
exactly that many ASCII characters, with no terminator and no padding; records are packed back
to back and are reached only through TOKEN_POINTERS_TABLE ($25DD), never by scanning.
The dictionary stores case-sensitive duplicates because prose is emitted verbatim: "the"
($2699) and "The" ($27CF), "to" ($26DB) and "To" ($2805), "There" ($26AB) and "there" ($2730),
"You" ($26D3) and "you" ($28B5) are separate tokens. Labels ending _LC or _CAP mark the
lower-case or capitalised member of such a pair.

LOAD_NEXT_GAME_PART ($9700)
Purpose: The runtime multipart loader, copied here from staging by ENTER_GAMEPLAY_DISPLAY. It puts the machine into a KERNAL-friendly state, blanks the display, names the next part file, runs the custom fast loader, then restores gameplay display, timer and interrupt state and advances the filename digit for the following call.
Inputs: None in registers. The inline five-byte filename at $9735 currently reads PART2; the drive must hold the disk.
Outputs: The named part is loaded over the overlay region; the inline filename's last digit is incremented so a later call requests the next part; the VIC display is re-enabled with a medium grey border, CIA 1 timer A is stopped, CIA 1 interrupt control is written with $10, $D01A is set to $F1 and $01 is returned to $36. Executable code occupies $9700-$9761; $9762-$98FF is installed tail and fill with no consumer.
Assumptions: Entered with interrupts about to be disabled by its own SEI. It sets $01=$37 so KERNAL ROM is visible for SETNAM, and leaves $01=$36 on exit, which is the gameplay configuration in which $A000-$BFFF is RAM. The filename increment is unconditional, so the routine is single-use per part in the order PART2, PART3, ...
Clobbers: A, X, Y, flags, KERNAL zero-page bytes $B9, $BA, $C3 and $FD, the inline filename byte at $9739, and the display, timer and interrupt state listed above.
Hardware changes: Executes SEI. Writes the 6510 port $01 ($37 then $36). Writes VIC-II $D011 (blank then enable), $D020 border, $D01A interrupt enable, $D019 interrupt latch. Writes CIA 2 interrupt control $DD0D and CIA 1 timer A control $DC0E and interrupt control $DC0D. Calls KERNAL SETNAM ($FFBD) and drives the serial bus through the custom loader.

ZERO_PAGE_BACKUP ($A000-$A0FF) - the game's shadow copy of zero page, swapped in and out
around KERNAL calls by SWAP_ZERO_PAGE_AND_BACKUP ($053C).
The game keeps its own working variables in zero page, which the KERNAL also uses. Rather
than saving individual locations, $053C exchanges the two 256-byte images wholesale: for each
index it loads the live byte, loads the backup byte, writes the backup value live, and writes
the live value into the backup. One routine therefore serves both directions - calling it
twice restores the original state - and there is no separate "restore" entry point.
053C  LDY #$FF
053E  LDA $0000,Y     ; live zero-page byte
0541  TAX
0542  LDA $A000,Y     ; corresponding backup byte
0545  STA $0000,Y     ; backup -> live
0548  TXA
0549  STA $A000,Y     ; live -> backup
054C  DEY
054D  CPY #$01        ; stop before index $01
054F  BNE $053E
C64 SPECIFIC, AND THE REASON FOR THE ODD LOOP BOUND: the loop runs Y = $FF down to $02 and
deliberately never touches $0000 and $0001. On a 6510 those two addresses are not RAM but the
CPU's on-chip I/O port - $0001 is the bank-select register that decides whether BASIC, KERNAL,
I/O or RAM is visible at $A000-$BFFF and $D000-$FFFF, and $0000 is its data-direction
register. Swapping a stale value into $0001 would change the memory map underneath the
running code, most likely unmapping the very routine performing the swap. Banking is managed
separately, by explicit stores to $01 (see $975D, which restores the game's standard $36 map
after a disk load).
Note the backup lives at $A000-$BFFF RAM, i.e. underneath the BASIC ROM image, which is
exactly the region the $01 value chosen by this game leaves as RAM.
The instruction operands establish the $A000 base. Ghidra records an `abs,Y` reference one byte above the base, so operand inspection is required. Byte evidence agrees: aligning $A000 with $0000 matches 198 of 256 captured bytes, against 80 when aligned at $A001. The 58 differences are expected because the backup is a prior zero-page snapshot, not a live mirror.

OBJECT_ICON_TABLE ($A560-$BBDF, 5760 bytes) - 36 fixed 160-byte slots originally allocated
to inventory and scripted-scene icons, laid out back to back with no header.
ADDRESSING
CALC_OBJECT_GRAPHIC_PTR ($0F70) computes the slot address as $A560 + $A0 * CURRENT_OBJECT_INDEX
by repeated addition, leaving it in GRAPHIC_RECORD_PTR ($5A/$5B). For normal inventory icons the index is the position at which the resolver at $15E3 found the
parsed noun key inside NOUN_TO_OBJECT_INDEX ($22A4). SCRIPT_SET_OBJECT_GRAPHIC ($113D) instead
reads an icon index directly from action bytecode, so a scripted scene can select a slot that no
parsed noun can reach. NOUN_TO_OBJECT_INDEX holds 36 entries before its $FF terminator at $22C8,
and 36 * 160 = 5760 lands the last byte on $BBDF, immediately below SAVED_BITMAP ($BC00). Table
extent and slot stride therefore corroborate each other.
PAYLOAD FORMAT - identical to a RoomGraphicRecord payload with width = 4 cells and
height = 4 character rows. The source stream is interleaved per character row:
32 bytes  bitmap      (4 cells x 8 scanlines)
4 bytes  screen matrix
4 bytes  colour RAM
------------------------------------------------
40 bytes per character row, 4 rows = 160 bytes per icon
BLIT_ROOM_GRAPHIC ($05BF) / COPY_BLIT_ROW ($0676) scatter those three spans to three different
destinations, which is why they are interleaved rather than stored as three flat planes.
C64 DISPLAY SEMANTICS (for a reader fluent in 6510 but not in VIC-II)
The picture band runs in multicolor bitmap mode: RASTER_SPLIT_PICTURE ($A7E3) sets $D011=$3B
(BMM=1, bitmap mode), $D016=$D8 (MCM=1, multicolor), $D018=$38 (video matrix $CC00, bitmap
$E000, both inside VIC bank 3) and $D021=$00. In that mode the VIC consumes TWO bitmap bits per
pixel, so horizontal resolution halves - each 8x8 cell is 4 double-wide pixels across - and the
colour of a pixel is selected by the bit pair:
00 -> background register $D021
01 -> high nybble of that cell's screen-matrix byte
10 -> low  nybble of that cell's screen-matrix byte
11 -> low  nybble of that cell's colour-RAM byte
Hence the 4 screen bytes and 4 colour bytes per row: they carry three of the four palette
entries for the four cells in that row. An icon is 32 x 32 screen pixels (16 double-wide
multicolor pixels wide).

and calls RENDER_ROOM_GRAPHICS ($0570) to repaint the band.

RASTER_IRQ_DISPATCH ($A7E0)
Purpose: The gameplay interrupt handler, installed in the KERNAL RAM vector CINV. A CLC followed by a BCC whose offset byte at $A7E2 is self-modified selects one of the three raster-split phase bodies, so successive interrupts cycle picture, text and bottom.
Inputs: The offset byte at $A7E2 holds $00, $27 or $52, selecting $A7E3, $A80A or $A835 respectively. The KERNAL's hardware IRQ entry at $FF48 has already pushed A, X, Y and the status register.
Outputs: The selected phase reprograms the VIC, arms the next raster compare, rewrites the offset byte for the following interrupt, acknowledges the VIC interrupt latch and chains to the KERNAL epilogue at $EA81, which pulls the registers and executes RTI.
Assumptions: Requires $01=$36 or another configuration in which $A000-$BFFF reads as RAM; banking BASIC back in while this vector is live would vector the interrupt into ROM. It relies entirely on the KERNAL prologue for register preservation, so it must never be entered by a foreground JSR.
Clobbers: A and flags within the handler; the interrupted A, X, Y, status, stack context and program counter are all restored by the KERNAL epilogue. The offset byte at $A7E2 is rewritten every interrupt.
Hardware changes: Through the selected phase: VIC-II $D011, $D016, $D018, $D021, $D012 and $D019. CINV itself is not modified here.

RASTER_SPLIT_TEXT_DELAY ($A80A)
Purpose: Phase body for the middle band, entered eight CPU cycles early. The dispatcher's $27 offset lands on four NOPs, which delay the register writes so that the picture-to-text transition happens at the intended horizontal position; the body then switches the VIC-II back to hires text, arms line 138 and selects the bottom phase.
Inputs: Entered from the dispatcher with offset $27, on the interrupt armed for raster line 130. The KERNAL register-save frame is present.
Outputs: Eight cycles consumed, then: background medium grey; screen matrix $CC00 and character generator $F800; text mode; multicolor off; next compare at line 138; dispatch offset set to $52; interrupt acknowledged; return through $EA81.
Assumptions: The delay exists because the interrupt is only line-accurate, not cycle-accurate; without it the mode change would land inside the visible part of the line. The character generator at $F800 is RAM that only the VIC-II can see, since the CPU has KERNAL ROM there under $01=$36.
Clobbers: A and flags; the offset byte at $A7E2. The interrupted registers are preserved by the KERNAL frame.
Hardware changes: Writes VIC-II $D021 = $0C (medium grey), $D018 = $3E (screen $CC00, charset $F800), $D011 = $1B (text mode, 25 rows, display enabled, Y scroll 3), $D016 = $C8 (40 columns, multicolor off), $D012 = $8A (line 138), then reads and rewrites $D019 to acknowledge.

Purpose: Phase body for the bottom boundary. It changes no display register: it simply arms the next compare back at raster line 49 and selects the picture phase, restarting the three-phase cycle for the next frame.
Inputs: Entered from the dispatcher with offset $52, on the interrupt armed for raster line 138. The KERNAL register-save frame is present.
Outputs: Next compare at line 49; dispatch offset reset to $00; interrupt acknowledged; return through $EA81.
Assumptions: Because the text mode set at line 130 must persist to the bottom of the screen, this phase deliberately leaves $D011, $D016, $D018 and $D021 alone. Its only job is to close the cycle.

RESTORE_SYSTEM_TO_BASIC ($A893)
Purpose: Hand the machine back to the KERNAL and BASIC ROMs in a state a stock C64 can survive: select a ROM-visible memory map, zero the low RAM pages, rebuild the KERNAL indirect vector block, re-run BASIC's vector and zero-page initialisation, and restore the stock IRQ handler.
Inputs: None. Physically located inside a dead object-icon slot, which is why it survives in the icon table region.
Outputs: $01 = $36; $0002-$0101, $0200-$02FF and $0300-$03FF zeroed (the STA $0002,Y loop runs Y=$00..$FF, so it spills two bytes into the stack page); $B2/$B3 = $033C (the cassette-buffer pointer) and $C2 = 3; the 32-byte KERNAL default vector table copied from $FD30 to $0314-$0333; BASIC's indirect vectors and zero page reinitialised through KERNAL $E453 and $E3BF; CINV ($0314/$0315) = $EA31.
Assumptions: $01 must be set first, because everything afterwards reads KERNAL ROM. Note the consequence for its own neighbourhood: with $36 selected, $A000-$BFFF still reads as RAM, so this code and the icon table around it remain reachable, while $E000-$FFFF is ROM, which is why the game's own character set at $F800 becomes invisible to the CPU though the VIC-II still sees it. No resident caller is recorded in the captured occupant.
Clobbers: A, X, Y, flags, the whole of zero page and pages 2 and 3, and BASIC's workspace. X is destroyed by the KERNAL calls to $E453 and $E3BF.
Hardware changes: Writes the 6510 port $01. Rewrites the KERNAL RAM vector block $0314-$0333 including CINV. Calls KERNAL $E453 and $E3BF. Does not itself touch VIC-II, SID or CIA registers, but restoring CINV to $EA31 hands interrupt-driven keyboard scanning and jiffy timing back to the KERNAL.

INSTALL_GAME_IRQ ($A8CC)
Purpose: Point the KERNAL RAM interrupt vector at the game's raster-split dispatcher and stop CIA 1 from raising its own interrupt. The exact inverse of the tail of RESTORE_SYSTEM_TO_BASIC.
Inputs: None. Also located inside a dead object-icon slot.
Outputs: CINV ($0314/$0315) = $A7E0; CIA 1's FLAG interrupt mask cleared; any latched CIA 1 interrupt request discarded.
Assumptions: Requires $01=$36 so that $A7E0 is the game's handler in RAM rather than BASIC ROM, and requires the raster source and initial compare to have been configured already. No resident caller is recorded, but CINV holds $A7E0 in the captured state, proving this routine or an equivalent loader path ran before capture.
Clobbers: A and flags.
Hardware changes: Writes the KERNAL RAM IRQ vector at $0314/$0315. Writes $10 to CIA 1 interrupt control $DC0D: with bit 7 clear the one bits are cleared, so this clears the FLAG mask and leaves the other sources alone. Then reads $DC0D, whose read side reports and clears the pending latch and releases the IRQ line, guaranteeing no stale CIA request fires when interrupts are re-enabled.
